spec.title: API Price & Stock Change Tracker

user_stories.story: As a dashboard user, I open the React app and see live stock prices update in real time without refreshing the page.
As a dashboard user, I can subscribe to one or more stock symbols and immediately receive their latest known price, then live tick updates as they arrive.
As a dashboard user, I can stop watching a symbol and the backend stops pushing updates for it to me.

As an operator, I can define a threshold rule (price above/below a value, or percentage move over a window) for a symbol so that when the condition is met, an external webhook is called automatically, without me polling anything.
As an operator, I need only one outbound connection to Finnhub regardless of how many browsers or symbols are active, because the free tier allows exactly one concurrent upstream websocket.
As a developer, I can run the full backend test suite with no network access and no real Finnhub/Redis/Postgres credentials, and it passes deterministically.
As a maintainer, every push/PR is automatically checked by CI (backend tests + frontend build/test) before merge, and no secret is ever committed to the repo.

acceptance_criteria.criterion: On FastAPI startup (lifespan "startup" phase), exactly one Finnhub websocket client connection is created. On shutdown (lifespan "shutdown" phase), that connection is closed. No code path outside the lifespan-managed client (e.g. no request handler) opens a Finnhub connection; a test asserts the upstream client is instantiated/connected exactly once for the app's lifetime even when multiple symbols/browsers are active.

A ConnectionManager class tracks connected browser WebSocket objects, can broadcast a tick to all (or to the subset subscribed to that symbol — see Assumption A1), and removes a connection from its tracking set when the send fails or the socket disconnects, without raising an unhandled exception or crashing other connections' delivery.

A SubscriptionManager ref-counts symbol interest across browser connections: subscribing a second browser to a symbol already subscribed by another browser does NOT send a second upstream "subscribe" message to Finnhub. Unsubscribing a symbol only sends an upstream "unsubscribe" message when its ref-count reaches zero.

When a browser WebSocket disconnects without sending an explicit unsubscribe, the SubscriptionManager decrements ref-counts for every symbol that connection was subscribed to, applying the same zero-count unsubscribe rule as criterion 3.
Subscribing to a symbol a connection is already subscribed to is idempotent: ref-count is not incremented twice and no duplicate upstream subscribe is sent.
On successful subscribe, if Redis holds a cached last price for that symbol, the subscribing browser receives that cached value immediately (snapshot) before/independently of the next live tick.

An API (REST and/or WS control message) lets a client create, list, and delete threshold rules (price-above, price-below, percent-change-over-window) scoped to a symbol; rules are held in an in-memory store that is the source of truth for real-time evaluation.

Every incoming tick is evaluated against in-memory rules for its symbol. A rule fires only on the transition into the triggering condition (edge-triggered), not on every subsequent tick that still satisfies it, so a sustained breach does not spam duplicate webhooks (see Assumption A4).

When a rule fires, the backend sends an HTTP POST (via httpx, async) to the rule's configured webhook URL with a JSON body describing the event, plus a header carrying an HMAC-SHA256 signature of the raw body computed with a secret from configuration. A test (fake webhook receiver) verifies the signature header is present and valid for the given secret and body.

Webhook delivery failure (timeout, connection error, non-2xx) is caught, logged, and optionally retried up to a bounded number of attempts; it never raises out of the tick-processing path and never blocks ingestion of subsequent ticks.

If rule persistence is enabled, created/updated/deleted rules are written to a Postgres table and reloaded into the in-memory store on startup; if the database is unavailable, rule CRUD and real-time evaluation still work in-memory and the error is logged rather than raised to the caller (see Assumption A5).

Incoming ticks are asynchronously persisted to a TimescaleDB hypertable (symbol, price, volume/size if available, exchange timestamp, received timestamp) without blocking or measurably delaying the browser-facing broadcast path; persistence failures are logged and do not stop the live pipeline.

All secrets and environment-specific values (FINNHUB_API_KEY, WEBHOOK_SIGNING_SECRET, DATABASE_URL, REDIS_URL, and any others introduced) are read only from environment variables / `.env`. A committed `.env.example` lists every required variable name with a placeholder (no real values). `.gitignore` excludes `.env` (and any local env files) from version control. A test or static check confirms no secret-shaped literal is hardcoded in source.

`docker-compose.yml` at the project root defines `redis` and `timescaledb` (Postgres+TimescaleDB image) services with the ports/env needed for local backend development, plus backend and frontend services wired to them via environment variables.

The backend pytest suite runs with no network access and without a real Finnhub connection: a fake upstream (in-process fake websocket server or a monkeypatched/injectable client emitting canned trade messages) stands in for Finnhub in all tests. `pytest` run from the backend project exits 0 with this fake in place and no live credentials.

GitHub Actions CI (`.github/workflows/ci.yml`) runs on push and pull_request with at least two jobs: (a) backend job that starts `redis` and `timescaledb` as service containers, installs Python deps, and runs `pytest`; (b) frontend job that installs Node deps and runs the frontend build and frontend test command. The workflow fails (non-zero) if either job fails.

The React frontend renders a dashboard that: lets the user add/remove watched symbols, displays updating prices for watched symbols received over a WebSocket connection to the backend, and provides a form to create alert rules via the backend rules API.

Reconnection: if the single upstream Finnhub connection drops, the backend attempts to reconnect with backoff and re-sends subscribe messages for every symbol that currently has a non-zero ref-count, without requiring browsers to resubscribe.

assumptions.assumption: Per-symbol fan-out: each browser WebSocket only receives tick messages for symbols it has subscribed to, not a global broadcast of every symbol being tracked by any client. This is the standard interpretation of "symbol subscription management" and keeps bandwidth proportional to each client's interest.

Market data provider is Finnhub via its public websocket (`wss://ws.finnhub.io`), auth via API key query param, using the `websockets` Python library for the upstream client (direct control over a single connection, as required) rather than an SDK.

Backend stack: FastAPI + Uvicorn, `redis` (async client) for the price cache, `asyncpg` for TimescaleDB/Postgres access, `httpx` (async) for outbound webhooks, `pytest` + `pytest-asyncio` for tests. Frontend: Vite + React, with Vitest + React Testing Library for frontend tests, built with `npm run build`.

"Volatility hit" rules are implemented as a percent-change-over-a-rolling-window check (e.g. price moved more than X% within the last N seconds/minutes), computed from either the in-memory last-seen price/time or cached Redis value plus current tick; exact window granularity is an implementation detail left to the builder as long as it is configurable per rule.

DB persistence of rules and ticks is "best effort": the in-memory rule store and the live broadcast/ingestion path are the source of truth and must keep working even if Postgres/TimescaleDB is down or slow; persistence is an added durability/history feature, not a hard dependency of the real-time path. Redis is similarly best-effort for snapshot-on-subscribe only, not required for ticks to flow.
A single shared `WEBHOOK_SIGNING_SECRET` env var is used to HMAC-sign all outgoing webhook payloads (per-rule secrets are out of scope unless trivial to add).
No authentication/authorization is required for the dashboard or its REST/WS API in this iteration (local/dev-focused build); this can be added later without changing this spec's scope.

Project files live directly under the existing project root (not inside a nested new folder), organized as `backend/` and `frontend/` subfolders plus root-level `docker-compose.yml`, `.env.example`, `.gitignore`, and `.github/workflows/ci.yml`.

edge_cases.edge_case: Finnhub upstream connection drops or errors mid-session: must reconnect with backoff and resubscribe currently ref-counted symbols (criterion 18) without dropping/corrupting ref-counts.

Rapid subscribe/unsubscribe/resubscribe of the same symbol by overlapping browsers must not cause ref-count to go negative or leave a phantom upstream subscription after the last browser truly leaves.
A browser subscribes to a symbol with no Redis cache entry yet (first time ever tracked): it simply waits for the next live tick, no error raised.
A rule's webhook endpoint is slow or unreachable: delivery must not block or slow down tick ingestion/broadcast for any symbol.
Redis is down when a subscribe happens: snapshot step is skipped/logged, live ticks still flow once they arrive.
Postgres/TimescaleDB is down at startup or during operation: app still starts and serves real-time data; persistence operations fail silently into logs (not exceptions surfaced to the client).

A rule condition remains true across many consecutive ticks (sustained breach): only one webhook fires per crossing (edge-triggered per criterion 8), re-arming only after the condition becomes false again (or per a defined cooldown), to avoid webhook spam.

Invalid/unknown symbol subscribed by a browser: backend forwards the subscribe to Finnhub as requested; if Finnhub never sends data for it, the browser simply receives no ticks for that symbol (no crash).
Multiple rules on the same symbol with different thresholds: each is evaluated and can fire independently on the same tick.

Server restarts: in-memory rules are empty until reloaded from DB (if persistence enabled) or recreated by clients; in-memory ref-counts start at zero and browsers must resubscribe after reconnecting their WebSocket.

risks.risk: The single-upstream-connection constraint is the core architectural risk: any bug in ref-counting or reconnect logic can either exceed Finnhub's one-connection limit (causing Finnhub to reject/kill the connection) or silently stop delivering data for symbols still wanted by active browsers.

A fake/mocked Finnhub upstream in tests may not faithfully reproduce real Finnhub message framing, auth handshake, or error/close behavior, so passing tests do not guarantee correct behavior against the live Finnhub websocket.

Edge-triggered rule firing (criterion 8) is an assumption (A4) about desired alerting semantics; if the real intent was "fire every tick while condition holds" or "fire once then auto-delete the rule," behavior will not match expectations.
HMAC webhook signing has no standardized header name specified by the request; an arbitrary but documented header/scheme is used, which downstream webhook consumers must be told about separately.

TimescaleDB-specific features (hypertables) require the Timescale extension to be enabled in the Postgres service image/init script; if the compose image or init SQL is misconfigured, persistence tests could pass locally but fail in CI's service container or vice versa.

dependencies.dependency: Finnhub websocket API and a valid FINNHUB_API_KEY (external, not used in automated tests — only in real/manual runs).
Python packages: fastapi, uvicorn, websockets, httpx, redis (async client), asyncpg, pydantic / pydantic-settings, pytest, pytest-asyncio.
Node/npm packages: react, vite, vitest, @testing-library/react (or equivalent) for the frontend.
Docker + docker-compose for local Redis and TimescaleDB (and optionally backend/frontend) services.
GitHub Actions runner with service containers for redis and a TimescaleDB-capable Postgres image.

spec.self_critique: Every user story maps to at least one acceptance criterion: live prices -> 2,6,17; subscribe/unsubscribe -> 3,4,5,6,17; threshold webhooks -> 7,8,9,10; single-upstream constraint -> 1,3,18; offline tests -> 15; CI/secrets -> 13,14,16. Each criterion is observable: either by direct unit/integration test (ref-count behavior, signature header, retry-not-blocking, fake-upstream pytest run) or by inspecting committed files (.env.example, .gitignore, docker-compose.yml, ci.yml contents and job definitions). None depend on subjective judgment. Biggest residual uncertainty: whether ticks should fan out to all connected browsers or only to those subscribed to that specific symbol (Assumption A1), and the exact alert-firing cadence (edge-triggered vs. every-tick vs. fire-once-then-disable, Assumption A4). Both were treated as assumable rather than blocking because a reasonable, clearly-stated default exists and the overall architecture (lifespan singleton upstream, ref-counted subscriptions, in-memory rules, HMAC webhooks) is unaffected by which choice is made — an implementer or reviewer can flip either behavior later with a small, localized change if the assumption turns out wrong.
